overview.body:
**Kotoshironushi** ​(*kotoshironushi*) — ‌Oracles, ‌Fishing · ​Lord ​who substitutes ​— ​belongs to ​the ‌Japanese tradition, ​where ​it is ‌catalogued ​under the ‌domain ​"Oracles, Fishing". ‌The ​name means ​"Lord ​who substitutes"[^1].

​**Kotoshironushi** ​is the ‌son ​of ‌Ōkuninushi who, ​according ‌to the ​*Kojiki*, ‌surrendered the ​central ‌land of ​reed ​plains to ‌the ‌heavenly descendants ‌of ​Amaterasu. A ​god ‌of oracles ​and ​fishing, he ‌withdrew ​to the ​sea ‌and became ​identified ‌in later ​tradition ​with the ​fortune ​god Ebisu.[^2]

‌PuniCodex ‌restores the ​name ‌as **Kotoshironushi** ​and ​serves its ‌temple ‌at [its ‌temple](https://punicodex.com/kotoshironushi/). ‌The restoration ​aSCII-equivalent ‌form — ​a ​description computed ​from ‌the ​displayed form ​itself. ​The plain ‌ASCII ​form *kotoshironushi* ​survives ​as a ‌modern ​convenience imposed ‌by ​the early ‌domain-name ​system; the ‌restoration, ‌not the ​fallback, ​is the ​form ​the project ‌defends ‌as philologically ​complete[^3].

the-name.body:
The ​name is ‌attested in ‌Japanese ​characters as ​**事代主神**. ​Etymologically it ​means "Lord ​who ‌substitutes"[^1].

The ​ASCII form ​*kotoshironushi* ‌survives only ​because the ‌early ​domain-name system ‌could ​not carry ​diacritics; it ​is ​a technological ​compromise, not ‌an ​ancient spelling. ‌The Unicode ​restoration ‌**Kotoshironushi** recovers ​the ‌full diacritic ​detail of ‌the ​scholarly transliteration ​directly in ‌the ‌address bar. ‌The restoration ​aSCII-equivalent ​form — ‌a ​description computed ​from the ‌displayed ​form itself.

​The letter-by-letter ‌transformation ​runs:

- **k** ‌→ **K** ​— ​Same, capitalized
- ​**o** ​→ **o** ‌— Same
- ‌**t** ​→ **t** ‌— Same
- ​**o** ​→ **o** ‌— Same

pronunciation.body:
The ​reconstructed pronunciation ‌of the ‌name ​is **/ko.to.ɕi.ɾo.nɯ.ɕi/** ​— ​Modern Standard ​Japanese (Hepburn).[^1]

​Phoneme ‌by phoneme:

- ​**Koto-** ​— Voiceless ‌velar [k], ​open-mid ‌[o], alveolar ​[t], open-mid ‌[o]; ​from 事 ​'matter/affair'
- ​**-shiro-** — ​Voiceless alveolo-palatal ​[ɕ], ‌close front ​[i], ‌alveolar tap ​[ɾ], open-mid ‌[o]; ​from 代 ‌'substitute/age'
- ​**-nushi** — ‌Alveolar nasal ​[n], ​close back ‌[ɯ], voiceless ‌alveolo-palatal ‌[ɕ], close ​front ​[i]; from ‌主 'lord/master'

​For ​the modern ‌speaker, ​the closest ​approximation is: ‌'KOH-toh-shee-roh-noo-shee' ​— the ‌'r' is ​a ​light tap, ​and ​the final ‌vowels are ‌soft.

​Kindred and ‌historical ​forms of ​the name:

- ‌**Japanese** ‌— 事代主神 ‌(Kotoshironushi-no-kami), “Lord ‌who ​Substitutes”
- **Father** ‌— ​Ōkuninushi, ruler ​of the ​earthly ‌kami
- **Mother** ​— ​Hayaakitsuhime, daughter ​of the ‌sea ​deity Ōwatatsumi ​(Kojiki)

​Kotoshironushi keeps ‌its restoration ​plain: ‌plain Hepburn. ​He is ‌a ​son of ‌Ōkuninushi ‌and a ​key figure ​in ​the transfer ​of ‌the land ‌to Amaterasu's ​descendants.

domains.body:
**Kotoshironushi** ​is the ‌son ‌of Ōkuninushi ​who, according ​to ​the *Kojiki*, ​surrendered ​the central ‌land of ​reed ​plains to ‌the ​heavenly descendants ‌of Amaterasu. ​A ‌god of ​oracles ​and fishing, ​he withdrew ​to ​the sea ‌and ​became identified ‌in ​later tradition ‌with the ​fortune ‌god Ebisu.[^1]

### ​Land ‌Transfer

His ​counsel ceded ​the ‌land of ‌reed ‌plains to ​the heavenly ​grandchildren ‌— the ​surrender ​that founded ‌imperial rule ​without ​a war ‌of ​extermination.

### Oracle ‌God

​His name ​means “lord ​who ​substitutes”: the ‌voice ‌that speaks ​the divine ‌will ​when the ​god ‌himself is ‌hidden.

### Fishing ‌Deity

‌A grandson ​of ‌the sea ​deity Ōwatatsumi, ​he ​withdrew toward ‌the ​water and ​became ​patron of ‌its catches.

### ​Ebisu ​Link

Nishinomiya’s ​Ebisu ‌— rod ​and red ‌tai ​in hand ‌— ​is his ‌smiling later ‌face, ​the only ​purely ​Japanese god ​among the ‌Seven ‌Gods of ​Fortune.

sources.citation: Nihon Shoki — the parallel account; the oracle age of Emperor Sujin.

symbols.body:
The ​iconography ‌associated ‌with ​Kotoshironushi ​concentrates in ​a ​small ​set ‌of ​recurring ​attributes, ‌each ​a ‌compressed ​statement about ‌the ​name:[^1]

- ​**Fishing ​rod** ​— ​The ‌attribute ​he ‌carries as ​Ebisu, ‌god ​of ‌the ​catch ‌— ​the ​tool ‌by ‌which fortune ‌is ​drawn ​from ‌the ​sea
- ​**Sea ‌bream ​(tai)** ​— ‌The auspicious ​fish ‌whose ​name ​puns ​on ​medetai, ‌“auspicious”; ‌Ebisu’s ​perpetual ‌catch
- **Oracle ​implements** ​— ‌The ‌divination ‌tools ‌of ​the ‌Miwa ​tradition ​— the ​“substituted” ‌voice ​of ​the ​hidden ‌god
- ​**Kakuremi ​(the ​hiding)** — ‌His ​withdrawal ‌into ​concealment ‌after ​the ‌cession ‌— ​the ​survival strategy ​of ​the ‌defeated ‌old ​order

mythology.body:
Kotoshironushi’s mythology is brief but ​pivotal: as a son of Ōkuninushi, ruler of ‌the earthly kami, he advised the peaceful cession of ‌the land to the heavenly line of Amaterasu ​and then withdrew from the world. His “hiding” ​let the imperial succession begin without the annihilation of ​the old order, and later ages gathered his ​memory into Ebisu, the beloved god of fishermen and ​merchants.[^1]

### The Cession of the Land (Kojiki)

Amaterasu ‌resolved that her grandson Ninigi should rule the ​central land of reed plains, and sent the warrior ​god Takemikazuchi to compel its ruler, Ōnamuchi — ‌Ōkuninushi — to yield. Ōkuninushi’s son Takeminakata answered the ​embassy with defiance, was defeated in a trial ‌of strength, and fled across the sea to Suwa. ​Then the Kojiki slows for the decisive interview: ‌Ōkuninushi asked his son Kotoshironushi what should be ​done. Kotoshironushi answered that the land should be given ​up to the heavenly grandchildren, and — his ​counsel accepted — he withdrew into concealment, kakuremi, and ​“the land was then at peace.” His mother, ​the Kojiki adds, was Hayaakitsuhime, a daughter of the ‌sea deity Ōwatatsumi, which is why his disappearance ​ran seaward. By choosing counsel over resistance, one ‌son of the old order ended a war that ​his brother’s arms could not have won — ‌and the mythology marks the cost exactly: the surrendering ​god simply vanishes from the story he made ‌possible.[^2]

### The God Who Hides (Nihon Shoki)

The ​Nihon Shoki’s parallel account deepens both the withdrawal and ‌the genealogy: it names Kotoshironushi’s mother a child ​of the sea deity, binding him to Watatsumi’s watery ​realm, and dwells on the hiding itself — ‌the kakuremi by which the god of the old ‌dispensation removes himself so that the new one ‌can begin. Japanese scholarship has long read the ​“hiding kami” as the mythic signature of cults that ​withdrew from the political centre: deities who lost ‌the argument survived by retreating into oracles, mountains, and ​the sea, keeping a voice precisely by surrendering ​a throne. The theme recurs across the early chronicles ‌— gods who conceal themselves and must be ​lured, cajoled, or divined back into relationship with ​the court. Kotoshironushi is the purest case: he is ‌the patron of every defeated thing that refuses ​to die, and his entire myth is an exit ‌that turned out to be a survival.

### The ​Oracle Lord of Miwa (Shrine tradition)

His very ​name — 事代主, “lord who substitutes for the matter” ​— was read by later generations as a ​title of the oracular god: the one who speaks ‌the divine word in place of another, and ‌so “substitutes” for the hidden deity behind the message. ​Shrine tradition around Ōmiwa, at the foot of ‌Mount Miwa in Nara prefecture — one of ​the oldest sanctuaries in Japan, where the mountain itself ​is the sacred body of the god — ‌links his lineage to the Miwa cult, through which ‌the will of the kami was delivered to ‌the court by divination and trance. Some scholars have ‌gone further and proposed identifying Kotoshironushi with Ōmononushi, ​the great kami of Miwa itself; the identification ‌remains a hypothesis, but a telling one. In the ​Nihon Shoki’s age of oracles, the troubled reign ​of Emperor Sujin — plagues, failed harvests, and divine ​warnings that had to be sought and obeyed ‌— taught that neglected gods of the land ​would speak until properly housed. Kotoshironushi’s specialty is precisely ​that: being the voice of the one who ​is absent.

### The Smiling God of Nishinomiya (Ebisu)

By ‌the medieval and early modern centuries, the hidden ​god had resurfaced as the most approachable of deities. ​The great shrine of Nishinomiya in Hyōgo prefecture ​identifies its kami with Kotoshironushi and calls him ‌Ebisu — “the prosperous guest” — the smiling god ​who carries a fishing rod and a red ‌sea bream, the tai whose name puns on medetai, ​“auspicious.” Every January the shrine fills with merchants ‌and fishermen for the Tōka Ebisu festival, when visitors ​buy lucky bamboo grass and invite the god ‌of the new year into their shops and ‌boats. Among the Seven Gods of Fortune, Ebisu is ​the only one worshipped purely as a native ​kami, without Buddhist, Daoist, or foreign pedigree. The transformation ​is one of the neatest survivals in Japanese ​religion: the son who advised his father to ‌surrender an empire became the guest who blesses a ‌shopkeeper’s ledger. The old order lost the land ​— and won the marketplace.

syncretism.body:
Kotoshironushi ​is a ‌nodal figure ‌connecting the ​land-transfer ​myth, the ​oracle cults ​of ​Miwa, and ‌the later ​Ebisu tradition. ​He ‌represents the ​old order’s ‌willing surrender ​and ‌the sea’s ​continuing bounty, ​and ​his identification ​with Ebisu ​— ratified ‌at ​Nishinomiya and ‌celebrated across ​Japan at ‌Tōka ​Ebisu — ‌is one ​of ‌the clearest ​cases of ​mythological condensation ‌in ‌Japanese folk ‌religion. Within ​the Seven ​Gods ‌of Fortune ​he keeps ​company ‌with deities ​of Buddhist, ​Daoist, and ‌Hindu ​origin, yet ‌remains the ​only member ​with ​a purely ​native genealogy. ‌Some ‌scholars have ​further proposed ‌identifying him ​with ​Ōmononushi, the ‌serpent-kami of ‌Miwa, which ‌would ‌bind the ​surrender myth ‌directly ​to Japan’s ​oldest oracle ​shrine; the ‌identification ​remains a ​hypothesis, but ​it shows ‌how ​completely the ​hidden god ​was ‌absorbed into ​the living ‌cult.[^1]

Kindred ​figures ‌in the ​PuniCodex cross-tradition ‌index include ‌[[aseratu|Ašeratu]], ​[[babaluaye|Ọbalúayé]], [[benzaiten|Benzaiten]], ​[[ea|Ēa]], [[hoderi|Hoderi]], ​and ​[[longwang|Lóngwáng]], each ‌linked through ‌sea / ​water.

cultural-legacy.body: Kotoshironushi ​is ‌rarely worshipped ‌under ​his ​own name ​today, ​but ​his ‌legacy is ​everywhere ​in ‌January: Ebisu, ​his ‌smiling ​later ‌form, presides ​over ​the ​first business ​of ​the ‌year ​at shrines ‌from ​Nishinomiya ‌to Osaka’s ​Imamiya. ‌The ​Tōka ‌Ebisu festival ​draws ​millions ‌of merchants ‌and ‌fishermen ​who ​buy lucky ‌bamboo ​to ​invite prosperity ‌into ​the ​new ‌year. In ​the ‌national ​myth, ​he is ​remembered ​as ‌the son ‌whose ​counsel ‌spared ​the country ​a ‌war ‌of extermination ‌— ‌the ​voice ‌of peaceful ​succession ​on ​which the ‌imperial ​line’s ​legitimacy ​partly rests. ‌And ​at ​Ōmiwa, before ​Mount ‌Miwa, ​one ‌of Japan’s ​oldest ‌sanctuaries ​keeps the ‌older ‌stratum ​of ​his story: ​a ​god ‌who hides, ‌and ​speaks.[^1]

archaeology.body: Ōmiwa ​Jinja in ‌Sakurai, ‌Nara ​prefecture — ​among ​the oldest ​shrine ​sites ‌in Japan ​— ​faces Mount ‌Miwa ​directly, the ‌mountain ​itself ‌revered as ​the ​shintai, the ​divine ​body ​of the ‌god; ​no main ‌hall ​stands ‌between worshipper ​and ‌peak. The ​site’s ‌antiquity ​is supported ​by ‌third-century Chinese ‌chronicles, ‌which attest ​the ​political ‌prominence of ​the ​Yamato region’s ‌great ​shrine ​cults, and ‌by ​the dense ‌concentration ​of ​kofun burial ​mounds ​in the ‌Miwa ‌area. ​At the ‌other ​pole of ​his ‌myth, Suwa ‌in ‌Nagano ‌preserves the ​Takeminakata ‌cult that ​the ​land-transfer ​story left ‌behind. ​Nishinomiya Shrine’s ​Ebisu ​identification ‌took its ​present ​form in ​the ‌early ​modern period, ‌but ​the shrine ‌claims ​older precedent, ‌and ‌the ​Tōka Ebisu ​rite ​is documented ​from ‌the ‌Edo period ​onward.[^1]

meditation.body: Kotoshironushi ​is the ‌theology ‌of the ​graceful ​exit. ​Every tradition ​must ​answer the ‌question ​his story ​poses: ‌what becomes ​of ‌the old ​order ‌when ​the new ​one ​arrives? His ​answer ​— counsel ‌surrender, ​then withdraw ‌— ​let both ‌worlds ​survive. ‌There is ​a ‌distinctly Japanese ​lesson ​in the ‌shape ‌of his ‌career: ​power that ​argues ‌with ​history loses, ​while ‌power that ​serves ​as its ‌voice ​endures. The ‌oracle-god ​who speaks ​for ​the ​absent deity ‌becomes, ‌centuries later, ​the ‌guest-god who ​blesses ​the shop: ‌both ‌are the ‌same ‌office, ​the sacred ‌made ​negotiable. In ​an ​age that ‌treats ​every ending ​as ​a failure, ‌the ​Lord ​Who Substitutes ​reminds ‌us that ​some ‌of the ​most ‌durable things ​in ‌a culture ‌are ​precisely ​the ones ​that ​stepped aside ‌at ‌the right ​moment.[^1]

kojiki-nihonshoki.body:
Japan's two earliest chronicles, the Kojiki (712 CE) and Nihon Shoki (720 CE), record Kotoshironushi in mythic narratives of cosmogony and imperial descent. The name appears in kanji logographs whose readings were later fixed by tradition.

The restoration Kotoshironushi preserves the romanized scholarly form derived from those classical sources.[^1]

sources.citation: Kojiki — the land-transfer episode (Ōnamuchi, Takeminakata, and the counsel of Kotoshironushi).

shinto-sources.body:
Shinto ritual texts, shrine records, and norito prayers preserve the cultic identity of Kotoshironushi. The kami is honored at shrines associated with oracles, and festival calendars perpetuate the name.

The Unicode form Kotoshironushi gives that ongoing tradition a precise digital address.[^1]

sources.citation: Kojiki — the land-transfer episode (Ōnamuchi, Takeminakata, and the counsel of Kotoshironushi).

buddhist-japanese.body:
Japanese Buddhist literature and art sometimes assimilate Kotoshironushi into Buddhist cosmology, mapping kami onto dharmic protectors and bodhisattvas. The honji-suijaku discourse provides a framework for such identifications.

The restored name Kotoshironushi appears in both Shinto and Buddhist contexts in the PuniCodex archive.[^1]
